problem: The trap says a VM on your laptop 'has pooling of hardware'. It does not. Resource pooling means one provider's pool serves many separate customers at the same time; a single user's VM on a laptop is one tenant on one machine. The sentence teaches the exact confusion (virtualisation = pooling) that the trap is supposed to warn against.
fix: Calling any virtual machine a cloud. A VM on your laptop fails all five: no provider pool shared with other customers, no network access from standard clients, no elastic capacity, no self-service and no meter. Carving several VMs out of one machine is virtualisation; pooling begins only when those slices are handed to different customers. Recite all five, then judge.

problem: The step says the ₹500-per-student-per-year fee is 'not metered per hour or per GB' and then awards c₅ = 0.5. Under the chapter's own rubric (1 fully holds, 0.5 partly, 0 not at all) a flat per-head fee with no usage metering is a full miss, so the credit contradicts the reason given and makes the total look generous.
fix: Measured service: the fee is flat ₹500 per student per year; nothing is metered per hour, per GB or per request, and no usage report reaches the customer. Credit c₅ = 0. Total then becomes 0 + 0 + 0.5 + 0 + 0 = 0.5 out of 5, that is (0.5 ÷ 5) × 100 = 10 percent, with one partial credit and four full misses. (If 0.5 is kept, the step must say what is partly metered — for example a per-student account count reported to the college.)

problem: 'a class of 60 cannot become 600 machines in 6 minutes' mixes students with machines and is hard to read; a student may think the 60 refers to servers.
fix: Rapid elasticity: the single server has fixed capacity, so a load of 60 students cannot grow to 600 within a few minutes, and no extra machines are created on demand. Credit c₄ = 0.

problem: 'Pooling needs a way to slice one physical machine into many isolated pieces' describes virtualisation, but slicing one machine into many pieces is not yet pooling; pooling is when those pieces go to different customers. Read alone, the sentence supports the wrong idea that any VM is pooled.
fix: Virtualisation is the machinery underneath. Pooling needs a way to slice one physical machine into many isolated pieces and hand those pieces to different customers, and elasticity needs the pieces to be created and destroyed in seconds.

problem: The answer says the meter supplies the signal for automatic scaling and that 'without metering, scaling is blind or manual'. Autoscaling is normally driven by monitoring telemetry (CPU load, queue length, requests per second), which is not the same thing as the metering used for billing, so the answer blurs two ideas.
fix: Answer: elasticity must raise and lower capacity automatically, and an automatic decision needs a live measure of demand — requests per second, queue length, CPU load. Measured service builds that same telemetry and also reports it, so the meter serves two masters: the scaling rule and the bill. Metering and monitoring usually share one stream of measurements, but the bill alone does not scale anything.
